criteria.description: Correctly substitutes the linear reward into J(pi).
Correctly pulls w outside the sum/expectation to identify mu(pi).

solutions.fullSolution: J(pi) = E_pi{sum_t gamma^t w^T phi(s_t,a_t)}. w doesn't depend on t or the trajectory, pull it out: J(pi) = w^T E_pi{sum_t gamma^t phi(s_t,a_t)} = w^T mu(pi).

criteria.description: Correctly explains step 3 as max-margin discrimination of the expert against seen policies.
Correctly explains step 4 as an RL subproblem and why alternation is needed.

solutions.fullSolution: Step 3: find w that makes the expert's mu(pi*) look better than every policy tried so far, by the largest margin t (max-margin classification). Step 4: given the current w, solve the ordinary RL problem for the optimal policy under that reward. One round isn't enough because a w from step 3 only discriminates against policies seen so far; the new pi_{i+1} might exploit a loophole. Adding it to the discrimination set next round closes that loophole, iteratively narrowing w.

criteria.description: Correctly applies the Bellman equation for Q to arrive at the advantage function.

solutions.fullSolution: f_theta,phi(s,a,s') ~= r(s,a) + gamma*V(s') - V(s). By RL-04's Bellman equation, r(s,a)+gamma*V(s') ~= Q(s,a) (for the actually-transitioned s'). So f_theta,phi(s,a,s') ~= Q(s,a) - V(s) = A(s,a), the advantage function. This is why training this functional form gives g_theta reward semantics and h_phi value semantics: the algebra forces f toward the advantage function.
